title: May crowning
hookLine: children crown a statue of Mary with flowers in May

lines: A HILL OF FLOWERS AT HER FEET.
cards: The procession is already moving down the aisle.

Children in their best clothes, some still in first Communion white, each holding a few flowers: grocery-store tulips, lilacs cut from somebody's backyard, one dandelion held very seriously by a small boy.
The flowers are laid at the feet of a statue of Mary until there's a small hill of them. Then one child climbs a step and sets a ring of flowers on the statue's head. People sing.
Somebody's phone is out. And for a moment the whole parish is looking at a child's hands.

teach.b: You met this one briefly, among the months and their themes. First, what it is. A May crowning is a popular devotion, not a required feast.
Parishes and schools hold one in the spring, often in May, the month Catholic custom gives to Mary: flowers for a mother, in the season of flowers. Second, why a child.
In Matthew's Gospel, children in the temple are shouting hosanna, and the chief priests are annoyed.

teach.h: OUT OF THE MOUTH OF INFANTS.
teach.b: Jesus answers them with a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise." The crowning puts that verse into practice.
The grown-ups could do it more neatly; they hand it to a child anyway. Third, why flowers and not gold.

teach.h: NOT EVEN SOLOMON IN ALL HIS GLORY.
teach.b: Jesus points to the lilies of the field and says, "not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed as one of these."

teach.h: A CROWN THAT WILTS, GIVEN ANYWAY.
teach.b: A crown of flowers is cheaper than a king's, and in that saying it outshines one. Catholics call Mary queen because her son is king, and the Council speaks of her exalted by the Lord as queen.
But the crown a parish gives her grows in backyards. Fourth, the line.

Some readers trace the title queen of the May to old spring festivals where a girl was crowned with flowers, and a hymn sung at some crownings calls Mary queen of the angels and queen of the May in one breath.
By week's end, the crown will be brown and drooping, and someone will quietly take it down. The gift doesn't have to last to be given.

how: Some Catholic parishes and schools hold a May crowning in spring: children bring flowers in procession, one child places a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the people sing Marian hymns.

games.q: you're in the temple. children are shouting hosanna, and the chief priests are annoyed. Jesus is asked if he hears them. what does he say?
o: tell the children to quiet down.
answer with a psalm about praise from infants.
games.why: "out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise." the crowning hands the crown to a child for the same reason.

practice: Look closely at a flower or plant near you, one petal, the edge already starting to fade, or picture the flower you'd bring; a dandelion counts.
If you pray, offer it to Mary with the opening of the Hail Mary, Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; if not, simply offer it to someone you'd like to honor, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: May crowning. A spring devotion where a child sets a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the parish sings. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Queen of Angels, a title from the Litany of Loreto.

carryVoice: Your line: queen of the may. Crowned by a child's hands, with backyard flowers. See you tomorrow.
